examples: If you decide to study abroad, you should start preparing early.
When the moment to depart finally came, I suddenly started to feel anxious.
If you're moving, getting rid of bulky garbage is a lot of work.
If the tournament is canceled, the entry fee will be refunded.
Once it gets to next week, it may already be too late.
fields.explain:
Used when: referring to the point in time when a decision is made or an event begins (本番、締め切り、出発、中止...), or when an action has already been decided on (V-辞書形).
The second clause often goes with: 準備する、手配する、覚悟する、～べきだ、～つもりだ、～ないと（いけない）.
The nuance is more decisive/personal than となると; more familiar and colloquial than となれば.
Unnatural if the second clause is a direct command to the listener in a formal context; a suggestion or mild volition is preferable.

• Main meaning: “If/when (something) becomes or is decided to be A, then B”. Emphasizes the point in time when the change of state or the decision is established.
• Nuance: leans toward the speaker's standpoint, often followed by the speaker's volition/suggestion/planned action in the second clause. A feeling of “now that the time has come, I have to…”.
• Scope of use: both hypothetical situations (もし～) and situations that are almost certain or already decided (いざ/いよいよ～). The second clause is usually a plan, a preparation, or a predicted consequence.
• Difference from ～となると/～となれば: となったら is casual and practical, often used with personal preparations; となると leans toward “when it comes to that…” with an evaluation/difficulty; となれば leans toward a general supposition and is more written.
fields.notes:
• “いざ～となったら/となると” is a very natural phrase to emphasize “when the time actually comes”.
• With time expressions: 今日・明日・来週・年度末 + となったら expresses “once it gets to…”.
• Intonation: となった「ら」 makes the sentence softer than となると; a post-decision feeling.
• When the content of A is an official announcement (会社の方針、中止等)、となったら shows “how to respond” from the speaker's side.
mistakes: Confusion with となると: a sentence emphasizing an objective issue is better with となると (例: お金がかかる“となると”が自然).
Use with adjectives: Aい/na + となったら is less natural; prefer event-like N/V.
Direct commands: 避ける with となったら in formal writing; replace with ～べきだ／～ほうがいい.
JLPT: Identify the personal nuance (となったら) vs objective (となると) vs general supposition (となれば).

fields.meaning: I hear that…, it is said that…
fields.connection: V/A plain form + とのことだ / N/Naだ + とのことだ
examples: I'm told that Mr. Tanaka is off today.
According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, there will be heavy snow tomorrow.
We have been informed that the meeting has been canceled, so please take note.
The person in charge has asked that the documents be sent tomorrow.
I hear he won't be able to come next week.
fields.explain:
Used to pass on objective information while keeping a polite distance from the source.
When conveying an indirect command/request: 「～するようにとのことです」 sounds polite and avoids direct pressure.
Sentences often end in ～とのことです (polite) in business writing.
Not used to state the speaker's own opinion or subjective evaluation; it only reports.

• A hearsay pattern (伝聞): conveys information indirectly from another source in a polite, neutral way.
• Often used in company announcements, emails, and the news: “～とのことです” is more polite than “～そうです”.
• The source can be added: ～によると／～から／関係者によれば + ～とのことだ.
• Difference from ～ということだ: ということだ is somewhat more direct and is also used when explaining rules; とのことだ is polite/diplomatic and emphasizes the source of information.
fields.notes:
• Negative/past structures stay in the plain form: 来ないとのことだ／終わったとのことだ.
• The source can be omitted when it is clear from context: （上司から）明日は在宅勤務とのことです。
• For long quotations, 「～ということだ」 can be used to emphasize an explanation, while 「～とのことだ」 is used to wrap up the information.
• Very polite variant: ～とのことでした（polite past, softens the sentence in reports).
mistakes: Using it for your own opinion → incorrect: 「おいしいとのことだ」 (when it is your own impression). Use 「おいしいと思う」 instead.
Leaving out the source in formal writing can be vague; add ～によると／～から.
Confusion with ～そうだ（様態） “looks like”: とのことだ is only used to convey information, not to describe sensory impressions.
JLPT: When the answer requires the nuance of “a work announcement/polite passing on of information”, choose とのことだ over そうだ/らしい.

fields.meaning: It is believed that…, it seems…
fields.connection: V/A plain form + とみられる / N/Na(である) + とみられる
examples: The death toll is believed to be 10, but the details are still being confirmed.
The main cause is believed to be deterioration of the wiring.
The company's sales for the next fiscal year are expected to head toward recovery.
A man believed to be the culprit was seen in the neighborhood.
The number of participants is estimated at about 300.
He is believed to have already left the country.
fields.explain:
Neutral, objective nuance: often used in headlines/news reports to avoid absolute assertions before a final conclusion is reached.
Natural combinations: 数字＋とみられる／原因は～とみられる／～に関与したとみられる .
Position: used as the predicate (at the end of the sentence) or as a noun modifier.
Avoid subjectivity: do not add personal emotions; if a softer nuance is needed, use ～とみられている／～とみられます .
Tense and aspect: present to state an evaluation that is currently accepted; past when stating an evaluation of a past event.

～とみられる expresses the idea “ is believed to be / is considered to be / is likely to be…”, showing an objective judgment, usually based on facts, figures, or expert assessment. It is a typical nuance of news and report style, reducing the speaker's subjective imprint.

•
Source of conjecture: indirect or combined evidence (figures, investigations, observations, experts).

•
Objectivity: uses an impersonal subject, often combined with 警察・専門家・当局・気象庁 in another clause.

•
Scope of meaning: estimates ( 約N＋とみられる), causes ( 原因は～とみられる), states ( ～にあるとみられる).

•
Reference JLPT level: N2–N1 (appears often in newspaper reading comprehension).
fields.notes:
•
Implied responsibility for information:
～とみられる allows reporting without absolute assertion, suitable during the investigation stage.
•
Quantity expressions:
約N＋とみられる／N超とみられる are common in statistics, economics, and natural disasters.
•
Cause-and-result clauses:
～が原因だとみられる／～に起因するとみられる are used when there is no forensic/technical conclusion yet.
•
Switching style: when writing academic reports, you can mix in と考えられる／と推定される to vary the nuance.
mistakes: Confusion with ～らしい: exam questions often set traps around the source of information. とみられる = objective evaluation; らしい = hearsay/rumor.
Confusion with ～とされる:
とされる has a stronger “normative/academic” character; it is not a temporary estimate.
Forgetting 「だ」 with N/na-adj: N/na＋ だ＋とみられる is the standard form in written language.
Overuse in everyday spoken language: everyday speech is better suited to ～ようだ／～みたいだ.
Using it for commands/volition: unnatural. Avoid combining it with a direct command in the second clause.
Not appropriate when the evidence is already certain: once the result has been confirmed, use a direct assertion instead of とみられる.

examples: We cannot lend anything out unless you present your ID.
Unless you contact us in advance, a cancellation fee will be charged.
We cannot proceed with the delivery unless we check the contract.
fields.explain:
Increase objectivity with ～ます／です; avoid direct commands.
Suitable for signs/regulations: 入室不可,立入禁止…

- Used to state a mandatory condition in instructions/procedures: if it is not met, the next step cannot be carried out.
- Highly normative; often appears in official notices, procedures, and safety control.
fields.notes:
• Conversational contracted form: ～なきゃ（い）けない/～ないと, but the formality nuance differs.
• In reading comprehension, headings such as 〜手続きの流れ・注意事項 often come with this pattern. meaning_vi: Unless ～, not ⏐ explain: Expresses the idea that if the first clause is not ～, the following action cannot be carried out.
The second clause is a sentence with a negative meaning. It often expresses the speaker's negative feelings. ⏐ examples: 1. やってみないことには、できるかどうかわからない。
You won't know whether you can do it unless you try.
2. 実物を見ないことには、買う気にはなれない。
I can't bring myself to buy it unless I see the actual item.
mistakes: Mistaking it for a sufficient condition: in fact it is only a necessary condition; even with A, it may not be enough for B to happen.
Forgetting で after N/A-na: Nでないことには／静かでないことには.

examples: I thought that as long as I didn't quit my current company, this kind of life would never change.
Apparently the cancer was quite advanced, and they were told there would be no chance of survival unless there was surgery.
It's not that I can't go, but I need to prepare today.
At this price, it's not that I wouldn't buy it.
It's not that I don't understand how he feels.
It's not that this problem isn't difficult.
It's not that I dislike sake, but I can't hold my alcohol.
fields.explain:
Often accompanied by conjunctions/modifiers that express a condition: けど／が／なら／とはいえ.
Often used to politely decline or to accept with reservation: “可能だが積極的ではない”.
With i-adjectives, the long form “〜くなくはない” is fine for the JLPT, but spoken language tends to use まあ/別に to express something similar.

• “It's not that… not…”, i.e., a partial/reluctant/conditional acknowledgment.
• An ambivalent nuance that avoids a definite assertion; it often implies “it's OK, but…/there is some, but…”.
• The meaning depends heavily on intonation and the clause that follows (concession, condition, limitation).
fields.notes:
• Rising intonation at the end strengthens the sense of “quite possibly”, while falling intonation strengthens “reluctance”.
• Combine with conditions such as “〜次第で／〜条件なら” to clarify the limits: 手伝わなくはないが、時間次第だ。
• Na/N require “でなくはない”; dropping で is grammatically incorrect.
mistakes: Forgetting “で” with Na/N: “静かでなくはない”.
Confusing “〜くはない” (only emphasizes the contrasting part) with “〜くなくはない” (double negative). Example: 高くはない ≠ 高くなくはない.
Using it for a strong affirmation → wrong nuance (this pattern is not definite).
JLPT trick questions: choosing among なくはない／ないことはない／なくもない; pay attention to the degree of certainty and the style.

rows: Emphasizes logic, slightly stronger than “なくはない”
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いから<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>いとは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない

examples: It's not that I can't eat spicy food, but I'm not good with it.
I can also understand how he feels, to some extent.
If I push myself, it's not impossible to make it in time.
It's not that I dislike quiet places, but I prefer the city.
Depending on the price, I might buy it.
fields.explain:
Politeness level: Neutral; usable both in conversation and in light written language.
Building a soft argument: Often used to make a partial concession before stating a contrasting condition/main point.
Common combinations: ～なくもないが／けど, ～なくもないと思う, ～なくもないかな.
Pragmatics: Avoids giving the impression of a definite assertion; suitable when you don't want to make a firm promise or want to save face.

• Main meaning: A double negative with a mildly affirmative sense: “it's not exactly that… not…”, “it's possible that…”, “it's not that bad…”.
• Nuance of hesitation/concession: The speaker does not assert strongly but acknowledges only to a certain degree, usually to leave a possibility open or to avoid saying it directly.
• Implied condition/context: Often used with “が／けど／なら” to state a condition or exception: ～なくもないが…
• Intensity: The degree of affirmation is weaker than “できる/ある/いい” and stronger than “わけではない”.
fields.notes:
• With な-adjectives and nouns, ではなくもない is more polite than じゃなくもない.
• Often used with adverbs of degree: 少し/まあ/わりと/条件次第で + ～なくもない.
• Rising intonation on “ない” helps emphasize “it's still possible/it's not that… not”.
mistakes: Confusion with ～わけではない: a sentence with ～なくもない carries a mild affirmation, not just a negation of exceptions.
Leaving out the condition that follows: ～なくもない usually needs a following clause to clarify the limits.
Using it where a clear commitment is needed can give a “half-hearted” impression.
Wrong form with i-adjectives: 高くない→高くなくもない (not 高いなくもない).

rows: Colloquial, concise; nuance close to ～なくもない.
Negates exceptions; weaker affirmation than the three patterns above.
Direct negation, without the mild affirmation of ～なくもない.

fields.meaning:
～というのは→驚(おどろ)き、意外(いがい)等(など)の感情(かんじょう)
Expresses a feeling of surprise at something beyond what one imagined
fields.connection: N / V/A plain form + なんて/とは（だ can be omitted after present-tense Na）
examples: I never dreamed that life in Japan would be this busy.
I didn't know that security at the summit would be this tight.
To think they won a 300-million-yen lottery! (I'm so jealous!)
“Those two are getting divorced?! They got along so well.”
Even the company president doesn't really know how well this product will sell.
Even if we ban the use of cell phones, there's no telling how many students will actually comply.

fields.meaning:
～の立場(たちば)からいえば/いっても→気持(きも)ち、考(かんが)え方(かた)
Contrast, from the standpoint of
fields.connection: N(standpoint) + にしたら・にすれば・にしてみれば
examples: Dyeing my hair brown is nothing to me, but to my grandparents it is apparently unforgivable.
Since they know the company's business is struggling, even the union probably can't demand a big wage increase.

My husband is transferred often. It's probably fine for him, since he chose the job because he likes it, but the children probably hate being made to change schools every two years. As for me, I understand that it can't be helped, but I feel down every time we move.

fields.meaning:
基準(きじゅん)になるもの、相手(あいて)の希望(きぼう)等(など)から離(はな)れないようにする
In line with
examples: If you walk along the train tracks for about 5 minutes, there's a park on the right.
Three months left until the exam. Let's study according to this plan.
In line with its educational policy of respecting individuality, A High School places importance on interviews even in its entrance exams.
At our travel agency, you can choose a tour that matches your wishes from among many plans.
“We are sorry that we could not live up to your expectations.”
Stylish restaurants lined the road along the sea.
This mistake is a matter that affects the company's credibility.
Since a person's life is at stake, please deal with this as the top priority.
He is involved in the new business and is in charge of market research.
Information related to privacy must not be released outside the company.
A person who may have been involved in the incident has been identified.
fields.explain:
Used in regulations/notices to emphasize seriousness: 安全に関わる、生命に関わる等.
The connecting form ～に関わって… helps introduce a related reason/consequence.
In conversation, to say “take part in (something)”: プロジェクトに関わる/関わっている.
Avoid overusing it when it only means “about/on the topic of”: in that case ～に関する／～について is more natural.

• Related to, having an influence on a field/target (broad, covering both good and bad effects).
• Implies a deep degree of involvement, sometimes with a nuance of “being mixed up in” (negative) depending on context.
• Often used with serious matters: 命・安全・名誉・権利・プライバシー・信用・成否.
• Difference from 関する: 関わる implies intertwining/influence, not merely a topic.
fields.notes:
• “命に関わる” is almost a fixed warning phrase (medicine, occupational safety).
• In investigations: “事件に関わる（人物・証拠）” = “involved/implicated”.
• To emphasize an active participating role: 関与する/携わる may also be suitable (with different nuances).
mistakes: Confusion with ～に関する/～について when only stating a topic.
Confusion with ～に関わらず (regardless of) because they share the same root verb 関わる.
Machine-translating it as “mixed up in” everywhere → easily gives an unnecessary negative nuance; consider the context.
